vignette:
Vinh's War

Vinh was eighteen when the IED detonated outside the checkpoint in Kandahar. He had enlisted at seventeen with his parents' reluctant consent, drawn by the promise of structure and purpose that his chaotic childhood in a resettled Vietnamese refugee community had never offered. The explosion came on his third patrol-a Tuesday morning that felt like every other Tuesday until the moment the world inverted. The blast threw him backward into a concrete barrier; his best friend Marcus, who had been standing two meters to his left, was killed instantly. Vinh remembered the heat, the ringing silence that followed, and the terrible clarity of Marcus's absence-the space where he had been. He remembered thinking, in the seconds after, that he should have seen it, should have positioned them differently, should have insisted they take another route. He should have protected Marcus. He was certain of this with the kind of certainty that didn't require evidence.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. The psychological ones metastasized slowly over the months that followed. Back home in Sacramento, Vinh moved through the world as though it were a minefield. Ordinary sounds-a car backfiring, a dropped pan in the kitchen, his mother's vacuum cleaner-sent him into a state of raw alertness that left him gasping. His body would spike with adrenaline before his mind caught up; his hands would shake for hours afterward. He came to believe that relaxation itself was dangerous, a lapse in vigilance that would cost him. Even in his bedroom with the door locked, even when he knew logically that nothing threatened him, his nervous system refused the message. He lay awake most nights, cycling through scenarios in which he had failed again, in which his inattention would kill someone.

The memories of the blast had a quality unlike anything else in his mind. When they surfaced-triggered by a motorcycle engine, a crowd, the smell of diesel fuel-they didn't feel like recollections at all. They felt like the event happening again, happening now, with a sensory intensity that made his ordinary memories of his eighteenth birthday or his high school graduation seem pale and distant by comparison. The rage that accompanied these memories was volcanic. He would find himself furious at people who had nothing to do with the war, angry at his mother for asking him to pass the salt, furious at himself for the rage itself, which only made it worse.

He had taken up photography before the deployment-a way to see the world through a controlled frame, to make sense of chaos through composition. But when he returned home, the camera became a tool of risk. He would position himself in dangerous places to get the shot: on highway overpasses during rush hour, in abandoned buildings with unstable floors, in neighborhoods where he knew he shouldn't be alone. His mother found him one night on the roof of their house, photographing the city lights. When she asked what he was doing, he couldn't articulate why the danger felt necessary, only that the adrenaline rush felt real in a way that nothing else did anymore. The photographs themselves were technically excellent-sharp, composed, emotionally raw-but they frightened her.

He had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere. The world had split into two categories: those who had been there, who understood, and everyone else-people who could not be trusted because they could not possibly comprehend what it meant to fail the way he had failed. His parents tried. His high school friends tried. But their concern felt like judgment, their questions like accusations. He found himself isolating, spending hours alone with his camera, and when he did venture into public spaces, he was hypervigilant, scanning for threats, certain that danger was imminent and that he would not be equal to it.

Three months ago, his mother found him researching ways to end his life. She did not cry, did not argue; she simply drove him to the emergency room and sat beside him through the intake. Now, at eighteen, Vinh sits in the waiting room of a trauma clinic, his camera at his side, terrified that talking about what happened will make it real again, and equally terrified that staying silent will kill him.
